Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try hard to control my emotions
never allow myself to feel or express anger

Threat.value: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

Memory.value: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
People are not what they seem

vignette: Dr. Leonardo Bianchi had always prided himself on his rational mind and sharp analytical skills, honed from years of practicing psychology. But it was precisely this confidence that made him feel shattered after the physical abuse he suffered at the hands of his romantic partner two decades ago. The memories still lingered in vivid snapshots - the sound of breaking glass, the stinging pain as she slapped him across the face, and the feeling of utter helplessness. Leonardo's recollections were disjointed and fragmented; when asked to recount what happened, he often became tongue-tied, like trying to thread a needle with trembling hands. This inability to piece together a coherent narrative only fueled his self-doubt and feelings of inadequacy - "I should have been able to protect myself," he'd mutter in despair. Lately, he found himself increasingly on edge around women, feeling a shiver down his spine when being alone with them or encountering crowded spaces. Transportation was another source of discomfort; just seeing someone ride a bicycle would send him hurtling back into the past, making him watchful and alert for potential threats. Leonardo tried to compensate by adopting strict control over his emotions - "Don't let your feelings get the better of you," he'd tell himself sternly. This habit had become ingrained in recent years; even when talking about seemingly trivial matters, he caught himself suppressing any anger or frustration that threatened to surface. He started dressing in ways that made him feel less conspicuous, avoiding clothes similar to those his partner wore during their tumultuous relationship. However, this stifling of emotions only intensified the threat that lurked around every corner. Nighttime was particularly harrowing for Leonardo; as he lay awake, checking and rechecking whether all doors were locked and windows secure, the shadows cast by moonlight danced menacingly on walls. During waking hours, his eyes roamed public spaces with an almost professional intensity - searching faces for hidden signs of malice. Leonardo couldn't shake the conviction that others were hiding sinister intentions beneath polished facades; a nagging distrust had taken root within him, poisoning relationships and friendships. "They'll just hurt me like she did," he'd convince himself during moments of isolation. As his hyper-vigilance escalated, memories continued to surface - photographs in his mind that replayed the painful scenes with heart-stopping vividness. In those moments, emotion would overwhelm image, suffocating him beneath its crushing weight. The recollections not only fed into his feelings of inadequacy but also made him question everything he thought he knew about human nature and relationships. Leonardo found himself increasingly entangled in a web of threat assessment, memories that haunted him like specters, maladaptive strategies to cope with those memories, and triggers that brought it all crashing down. For years, this labyrinthine dance had kept him from forming genuine connections or engaging in his work as he once did. And so, at 68, after two decades of running on the hamster wheel of pain, Leonardo finally sought help - hoping to untangle himself from these paralyzing fears and reclaim a semblance of peace in his twilight years.
